questions.q: Per this lesson, why is a compromised integration credential potentially more dangerous than a compromised human user's login, not just equally risky?
options: Integration credentials always have unlimited API call volume, while human logins are rate-limited
There's no human present to notice something unusual and react, so misuse can continue unattended for a long time before anyone looks
Integrations are never covered by any Salesforce security feature, while human logins are
Integration credentials cannot be revoked once issued
questions.explain: The core premise of this lesson is that a human login depends on a person being present to notice something wrong; an integration runs on a schedule with nobody watching, so a compromised credential can be abused far longer before detection.

questions.q: This lesson names four places where an integration's real risk sits. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
options: The network path the callout travels across
The identity (user or certificate) making the call
The specific font or theme used in the Salesforce UI
Credentials at rest
questions.explain: The four risk areas are credentials at rest, the network path, the identity making the call, and the endpoint itself. UI styling has no bearing on integration security.

questions.q: A team scopes a new integration user with broad access to several objects 'just in case it needs more later, to avoid support tickets.' What does this lesson say is wrong with that reasoning?
options: Nothing -- broader access always makes integrations more reliable
It inverts the actual risk: an over-permissioned credential's blast radius is available to anyone who ever gets hold of it, not just the original intended use
It's fine as long as the integration user's password is strong
Salesforce technically prevents integration users from being granted broad access
questions.explain: A human user's over-permissioning is bounded by that one person's choices; an over-permissioned integration credential is available to anyone who later obtains it, so the blast radius of a compromise is exactly what that credential is permitted to do.

questions.q: In the realistic attack chain described in this lesson (hardcoded credential exposed in a public repository), what made the resulting data export particularly hard to notice?
options: The export happened through the API rather than the UI, so there was no familiar login screen for anyone to notice
The attacker used a VPN, which Salesforce cannot detect under any circumstances
Salesforce does not log any API activity
The integration user had no password at all
questions.explain: The scenario specifically notes that logging in as the integration user over the API, rather than through a UI login screen, meant there was no obvious login prompt for anyone to notice -- which is exactly why unattended API access needs its own monitoring, covered later in this course.

questions.q: What is a 'blast radius,' as this lesson defines the term?
options: The maximum number of records a single SOQL query can return
The scope of damage possible if a given credential or identity is compromised, determined entirely by what that credential is permitted to do
The physical distance a Salesforce data center can serve without failover
The number of connected apps registered in an org
questions.explain: Blast radius is defined in this lesson's Key Terms as the scope of damage possible from a compromised credential or identity, which is set entirely by that credential's granted permissions -- the less it can do, the smaller the blast radius.
